title: Pandit Girdhari Holds a Meeting
body: Pandit Girdhari Lal, pleader and Congress man, proposes to address a public meeting on the subject of the salt tax, self-rule, and — the intelligence report notes with alarm — ‘the general condition of things.’ It is entirely peaceful. It is also entirely legal. Both facts are considered a nuisance.

choices.label: Ban the meeting under Section 144. Order is order.
choices.outcome: The meeting does not happen. The reason it did not happen is now a far more effective piece of Congress propaganda than the meeting could ever have been. The Pandit sends you a note of thanks. You suspect he is not joking.

choices.label: Permit it, and send a clerk to take dull notes.
choices.outcome: Nothing happens. Speeches are made, the crowd disperses for tea, and the whole apparatus of sedition proves to run, like everything else here, on the assumption that it will be tolerated.

choices.label: Attend personally and sit in the front row.
choices.outcome: Your presence is so unexpected that the Pandit revises his speech on the spot to be scrupulously polite. You understand perhaps one word in five, and both of you leave convinced you have won.

title: Lala Hukum Chand Pays a Call
body: Lala Hukum Chand — moneylender, landholder, and the man to whom most of the district is quietly mortgaged — calls to pay his respects. He brings a basket of remarkable mangoes and mentions, in passing and with great delicacy, that a certain land dispute might be settled ‘to everyone's satisfaction’ with a word from your court.

choices.label: Accept the mangoes; ignore the hint.
choices.outcome: You have eaten the mangoes and taken none of the meaning, which the Lala finds both admirable and slightly stupid. He will try again, better, later.

choices.label: Decline the mangoes and the man, coldly.
choices.outcome: Incorruptible and lonely. The Lala's money oils every wheel in the district, and you have just introduced a little sand. Things will run slower now, and you will not know why.

choices.label: Have the mangoes; drop a helpful word in court.
choices.outcome: The dispute is settled to the Lala's satisfaction. You are now, in a small and deniable way, his. It is astonishing how light the first thread feels.

title: Deputy Collector Mukherjee Is Right Again
body: Sub-Deputy Collector Mukherjee — your Indian deputy, Cambridge-educated, visibly cleverer than you, and far too well-mannered to say so — points out, very gently, that the drainage scheme you approved yesterday will flood the very quarter it was meant to protect. He is, of course, correct.

choices.label: Thank him publicly and change the scheme.
choices.outcome: The scheme is fixed. The clerks note that the Magistrate takes correction from an Indian officer, and file the observation somewhere it may one day be useful to somebody.

choices.label: Change the scheme; take the credit yourself.
choices.outcome: The quarter stays dry and your reputation stays high. Mukherjee says nothing, and remembers everything, and remains more competent than you, which is the one thing you cannot fix.

choices.label: Overrule him. A sahib does not reverse himself before the office.
choices.outcome: The quarter floods on schedule. You were right about appearances and wrong about drainage, and the water does not care which.

title: The Long Evening
body: It is nine o'clock, the punkah has stopped because the punkah-wallah has fallen asleep, and you are alone in a bungalow the size of a barn with a bottle of Scotch and eleven hundred miles between you and anyone who knew you before India. The bottle, at least, is company.

choices.label: Pour a large one. And another. It is that or the silence.
choices.outcome: The evening softens. So, over the months, does something else. This is how the district's more famous ruins began — not with a scandal, but with a nightcap that grew steadily larger and started earlier.

choices.label: Pour a small one and write letters home you won't post.
choices.outcome: You describe an India that does not exist to people who would not understand the one that does. It helps. The unsent letters go in the drawer with the others.

choices.label: Go to bed sober and lie awake in the heat.
choices.outcome: Virtue, and the ceiling, keep you company until two. In the morning you are correct, upright, and hollow-eyed, which the office takes for dedication.

title: A New Form Is Required
body: Simla, in its wisdom, introduces Form XIV-B, to be completed in quintuplicate, recording the caste, occupation, and ‘general disposition’ of every petitioner appearing before the court. Ram Autar, your head clerk, lays it before you with the particular stillness he reserves for orders that are both compulsory and insane.

choices.label: Implement it fully. An order is an order.
choices.outcome: The office vanishes beneath quintuplicate. Justice slows to the speed of carbon paper. Simla, receiving its forms on time, concludes that Chhota Nagra is a model of efficiency, which is the exact opposite of the truth and precisely what the forms were designed to produce.

choices.label: Have Ram Autar fill them in plausibly and file the rest.
choices.outcome: Ram Autar's face does not move, but something in the office relaxes. A quiet compact is formed: he will manufacture the paperwork the Empire requires, and you will not ask how. It is the most useful alliance you will make in India.

choices.label: Write to Simla objecting to Form XIV-B on principle.
choices.outcome: You receive Form XIV-B-1, a supplementary form on which to record objections to Form XIV-B. The machine has met your resistance and grown a new part to digest it.

title: Ram Autar Has a Nephew
body: Ram Autar, your invaluable head clerk, mentions with exquisite indirection that his sister's son is a promising young man in want of a clerkship, and that a vacancy happens to exist in the tahsil office. Everything Ram Autar does for you depends on a web of exactly such small arrangements. So, you are beginning to realise, does everything.

choices.label: Appoint the nephew. Ram Autar has earned it.
choices.outcome: The nephew is appointed and turns out to be perfectly competent, which is not the point. The point is that you now understand how the district is actually staffed, and that the answer has nothing to do with the rules and everything to do with Ram Autar.

choices.label: Insist on open competition for the post.
choices.outcome: You hold a fair examination, which the nephew wins anyway, having been the only serious candidate Ram Autar permitted to apply. You have upheld a principle and changed nothing, at some cost to a friendship you could not afford to spend.

title: A Letter from the Hills
body: The hot weather is on, the plains are an oven, and a letter comes down from the hill station where your wife has taken the children for the season. She asks, not for the first time, when you will come up for your local leave — and whether it is not time the boy was sent Home to school in England, as everyone’s children are.

choices.label: Take your local leave and go up to the hills.
choices.outcome: A fortnight of cool air and your own family, and of pretending you are not thinking about the district. You come down restored and faintly guilty. The work waited; it always waits; that is the one dependable thing about it.

choices.label: Stay at your post; agree the boy goes Home.
choices.outcome: You sign the letter that sends your son across an ocean to be raised by a school and an aunt, for his health and his accent and his prospects. It is what the Service does to its families. You tell yourself it is for the best, and go back to the files.

choices.label: Stay, and put the decision off another year.
choices.outcome: You write a warm, evasive letter and post it up the hill. Nothing is decided, which is its own kind of decision. The heat presses on the bungalow like a hand.

title: The Hot Weather
body: By May the thermometer stands at a hundred and ten in the shade, the station has half-emptied for the hills, the punkahs never stop, and the nights are worse than the days. This is the season that breaks men quietly — the loo wind, the glare, and the long solitary evenings with nothing between you and the silence but a bottle and the ceiling.

choices.label: Keep to a rigid routine — dawn rides, cold baths, work.
choices.outcome: Discipline is the sahib’s armour against the heat. You ride at dawn, work through the shuttered day, and hold yourself together by the timetable. It is joyless, and it works.

choices.label: Let the Club and the bottle carry you through.
choices.outcome: The little society of the half-empty station closes ranks around its bar. The evenings pass more easily; the mornings less so. It is the well-worn road, and you can see from here where it leads.

choices.label: Drive yourself at the work to fill the emptiness.
choices.outcome: You bury the silence under files and clear a backlog two years deep. Simla is pleased. Something in you is being spent that no honours list will ever repay.

title: Lala Hukum Chand Calls It In
body: The mangoes are long eaten, and the Lala has come to collect on the goodwill he so carefully planted. Nothing so crude as the money, he assures you — merely a small matter: a rival trader whose licence might be found irregular, a word in the right ledger. He smiles. Outside, the district you both govern goes about its business, not knowing which of you it belongs to.

choices.label: Do the small thing he asks. It is small.
choices.outcome: The rival's licence is found wanting; the Lala's ledger is squared; a little of your debt is quietly forgiven. It was small, exactly as he said, and that is how it is done — never one large sin, always a series of small ones, each easier than the last.

choices.label: Refuse him, and let the debt stand.
choices.outcome: You decline, politely, and watch the warmth leave the room. The debt is called to its full figure, and his money leaves the wheels of your district un-oiled overnight. You have kept your honour. It will prove a more expensive possession than you imagined.

choices.label: Repay him in full from the chest and be free.
choices.outcome: You empty a dangerous share of the treasury to buy back your own hands. The Lala takes his money with a bow that conveys precisely how much more useful the debt would have been to him than the cash. You are poorer, and free, and those turn out to be connected.

title: The District Stops Work
body: What began with Pandit Girdhari's banned meeting has become a hartal — the shops shuttered, the courts empty, the very peons of your own cutcherry finding urgent reasons to be elsewhere. It is disciplined, it is peaceful, and it frightens the Secretariat far more than a riot would, because a riot can at least be charged.

choices.label: Break the strike under the emergency powers.
choices.outcome: You invoke the ordinances, arrest the organisers, and reopen the shops at the point of persuasion. Order returns to the surface of things. Underneath, something has changed no ordinance addresses: the district has learned it can stop, all together, whenever it chooses.

choices.label: Wait it out and let the hartal exhaust itself.
choices.outcome: You do nothing, magnificently, for eleven days, while Simla's telegrams grow shriller. The strike ends of its own weight, having proved its point precisely by your inability to prevent it. Blyth-Curram will remember that you sat on your hands. So will the Pandit.

choices.label: Meet the Pandit and offer a real concession.
choices.outcome: You do the thing no one in Simla forgives: you treat with him as a man with a case. You give a little — a committee, a hearing, a grievance actually addressed — and the shutters go up. You have kept your district and quite possibly ended your career, and you are no longer sure those are different things.

title: What Ram Autar Knew
body: An anonymous petition, in a clerk's careful hand, lays out how the head clerk's small arrangements have grown over the years into something the audit would call embezzlement and the district calls simply how things are done. Ram Autar has run your office, saved your reputation a dozen times, and, it seems, taken his tithe of all that passed through it. He awaits your decision with the stillness he shows a compulsory order.

choices.label: Bury the petition. He has earned that much.
choices.outcome: You feed the petition to the brazier and say nothing. The office runs on as before, and you understand at last that you did not buy Ram Autar's loyalty — you rented it, and this is the rent. He pours your tea next morning exactly as always. You cannot meet his eye; he does not require you to.

choices.label: Confront him privately and demand it stop.
choices.outcome: You put it to him quietly and he neither denies nor apologises; he simply, gravely, agrees. The skimming stops. So does a great deal of the frictionless magic by which your office used to work, for it turns out the two ran through the same quiet pipes.

choices.label: Report him. The law is the law.
choices.outcome: You do the clean, correct, ruinous thing. Ram Autar is suspended pending enquiry, and within a fortnight you discover how much of the district lived in his head and nowhere else. You have upheld the law and lost the man who made your rule possible. The files are honest now. They are also three weeks behind.

title: A Letter from the School
body: A letter comes, months old, in a round schoolboy hand already becoming a stranger's. Your son is well, is learning Latin, has been caned once (unjustly), and asks — without quite asking — when you are coming Home. Between the lines a housemaster has added that the boy is settling, which is the word the English use for a wound that has stopped bleeding.

choices.label: Write back at once, warmly, and promise a visit.
choices.outcome: You fill a page with a leave you cannot yet take and a green English field he half-remembers. It costs nothing to promise and steadies you to imagine it. Whether the promise survives contact with the Secretariat's leave-sanction is another year's grief.

choices.label: Send money and a stiff word of encouragement.
choices.outcome: You do what your own father did, in the same climate, for the same reasons, and tell yourself it made a man of you. The letter is correct and cold, and you know it even as you seal it, and you seal it anyway. The heat presses on the bungalow like a hand.

choices.label: Pour a drink and leave it unanswered.
choices.outcome: You mean to answer it tomorrow. Tomorrow the district has a fresh demand, and the letter migrates to the drawer with the others you mean to answer, and something between you and the boy lengthens by another silence. This, too, is how it is done.
